Tesla showed a Roadster that hovers on compressed-air thrusters, won't land until 2028, and the stock popped. The same morning, CoreWeave's credit default swaps hit distress levels. I can't think of a tidier pair of headlines for how differently two markets are reading the same year.

Stock investors price a story, and a flying car is a very good story. Bondholders price the cash that arrives on specific dates. CoreWeave is a company that rents out GPUs and funds them with debt. Its equity can run on enthusiasm for years. Its bonds only need the rent to cover the interest, and when they sell off, the arithmetic is the thing being tested. Reuters put it as a "test of the market's math," which is about right.

Look at the thread from the last month: SoftBank's jumbo junk deal, Oracle's force majeure notice, Broadcom lending Anthropic money to lease Broadcom chips. Then this week the chip stocks cracked. The equity side seems to be catching on to what the credit side was already pricing. Saxo's headline today describes a meltdown with a late recovery, and the recovery is the part I'd be wary of. It's what a market does before it decides whether this was a wobble or a repricing.

Indonesia is the same lesson in miniature. Its worst day since 1998, on a threat of expulsion from MSCI indexes, after the government reportedly put around $5 billion behind its own market. If you prop up a price, it tells you what you can afford to hold up, and it also tells everyone where the floor was never really there.

Warsh, meanwhile, declined to give a signal. Fair enough. Everyone else is giving one.
